article.title: JFrog Uncovers 54 Fabricated SQLite CVEs as 'LLM Slop,' NVD Marks Two Records Rejected
article.summary: JFrog found that 54 of 55 SQLite vulnerability disclosures from one GitHub account were AI-fabricated; NVD has since marked two of the CVEs as rejected.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Security researchers at [JFrog](https://research.jfrog.com/post/sqlite-critical-cves-or-llm-slops/) say a newly created GitHub account published a batch of SQLite vulnerability advisories that turn out to be almost entirely fabricated by an AI model, and the National Vulnerability Database has since marked two of the specific CVE records the firm examined as "Rejected." JFrog's investigation, covered separately by [LWN.net](https://lwn.net/Articles/1086936/), found that of 55 advisories published by the same account, only one described a real bug.

## What We Know

According to [JFrog Security Research](https://research.jfrog.com/post/sqlite-critical-cves-or-llm-slops/), a GitHub repository called "programmervuln/cveadvisory-" published a set of SQLite advisories "as part of other 50+ CVEs which we believe are also LLM slop except from one." The reports were not ignored on arrival: "NVD quickly flagged these as critical, and CISA's ADP agreed," JFrog wrote.

When JFrog examined the six SQLite-specific advisories in that batch, the firm said it found the same pattern in each one: the functions or line numbers cited did not exist in the SQLite versions the reports claimed to affect, and none of the proof-of-concept exploits triggered a crash. For CVE-2026-51302, JFrog wrote that "the primary issue is that exprComputeOperands() didn't exist in SQLite 3.41. It was added in the middle of 2025," and that the function said to be vulnerable, sqlite3ReleaseTempReg(), "do not involve heap deallocation" at all, "making a UAF impossible by design." For CVE-2026-51303, JFrog said, "A diff between 3.51.2 and 3.51.3 shows absolutely no changes to src/expr.c." For CVE-2026-51300, the cited line numbers turned out to be "a comment and a memory allocation call" unrelated to the claimed flaw. CVE-2026-51297 and CVE-2026-51296 both referenced functions or line numbers JFrog said do not exist in the target version, and CVE-2026-51304 described a function signature that, per JFrog, "does not exist."

JFrog said it tested each claim by cloning SQLite's own repository, checking out the affected release tags — "version-3.41.0, version-3.51.2, and version-3.51.3" — compiling them in isolated Docker containers, and running each advisory's proof-of-concept SQL "under AddressSanitizer (ASan) instrumentation." None produced a crash. The firm also ran the advisories through an AI-content detector, reporting that "All advisories in this repo seem AI generated when testing them with Gptzero."

Severity ratings shifted as scrutiny increased. JFrog said Red Hat initially assigned CVE-2026-51302 a "10.0 Critical severity score" before revising it. Red Hat's own advisory page now lists a CVSS score of 7.6 for that CVE and states that "SQLite upstream have confirmed this CVE as fictitious. No patches or errata are required, and customers may safely treat scanner findings for this CVE as a false positive," according to [Red Hat](https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/CVE-2026-51302).

The National Vulnerability Database has since acted on at least two of the six SQLite CVEs JFrog examined. Records for both [CVE-2026-51302](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-51302) and [CVE-2026-51296](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-51296) now carry the status "Rejected," each stating: "This record was withdrawn by its CNA. Further investigation showed that it was not a security issue."

Looking across the full set of advisories tied to the account, JFrog said "a broader audit of 55 advisories published by the same GitHub account revealed that 54 were completely fabricated, while one contained a real bug wrapped in unverified CVE metadata." The firm said it reported its findings "to GHSA, Redhat and NVD to assist in the remediation of these records," according to [JFrog Security Research](https://research.jfrog.com/post/sqlite-critical-cves-or-llm-slops/). JFrog warned that "these LLM slop CVEs can cause organizations to waste time investigating and patching vulnerabilities that do not actually exist, as well as polluting vulnerability databases," and that the risk compounds "in environments where AI is used to automate vulnerability triage and remediation," since "an AI agent that encounters a fabricated CVE may attempt to locate the vulnerable function, generate a patch, or recommend changes based on code that does not even exist."

## What We Don't Know

JFrog's writeup does not identify who operates the "programmervuln/cveadvisory-" GitHub account or why the advisories were submitted. It is also not yet clear whether NVD or MITRE will formally reject the remaining four SQLite CVEs JFrog examined, or how the roughly 50 other advisories tied to the same account — covering software beyond SQLite — have been handled by the projects they targeted.

## Analysis

JFrog traces part of the problem to how vulnerabilities reach public databases in the first place. The CVE submission process, the firm said, "lacks any real identity verification, meaning virtually anyone can submit a vulnerability description and propose a CVSS score." It also pointed to a structural gap that predates the current wave of AI-generated reports: the National Vulnerability Database used to have "experts at the National Vulnerability Database manually analyzing and validating incoming CVEs," JFrog said, "but that safety net broke in February 2024." The result, per JFrog, is a pipeline where "no step in today's system actually requires a proof-of-concept or bug reproduction," letting "a plausible-sounding fake advisory" slide through unchecked — a gap the firm argues becomes more dangerous as AI tools are increasingly used to triage and act on vulnerability reports automatically.
